Where it began

Brian Lara was born in Santa Cruz, Trinidad, on 2 May 1969, one of eleven siblings. His family signed him up for Sunday coaching at a local clinic when he was six, so the textbook basics came early. At Fatima College he flourished, and at 14 he scored 745 runs in the schoolboys' league at an average of more than a hundred.

In 1987 he broke the run record at the West Indies Youth Championships and captained Trinidad and Tobago to the title. A year later he made his first-class debut, and in only his second game he took 92 off Barbados, whose bowlers included Joel Garner and Malcolm Marshall. At 20 he became Trinidad and Tobago's youngest captain.

The player

His first Test came against Pakistan in 1990, and his first Test hundred, in his fifth match, was 277 at Sydney in 1993. In 1994 he made 375 against England, a new world record for a Test innings. It began a run of seven hundreds in eight first-class innings, and the last of them was 501 not out for Warwickshire against Durham, a world record in first-class cricket. When Matthew Hayden passed his Test mark in 2003, Lara took it back the following year with 400 not out against England, the only man ever to reclaim it.

In all he played 131 Tests from 1990 to 2006, making 11,953 runs at 52.89 with 34 hundreds, nine of them doubles. He held 164 catches and led West Indies in 47 Tests, and in 2004 captained them to the Champions Trophy.

What made him special

Lara batted with flair and a hunger for runs that seemed to have no ceiling. When he got in, the bowlers knew they were in for a long day, and often a long week. His unbeaten 153 to win a Test against Australia in Barbados in 1999 was later ranked by Wisden as the second-best Test innings ever played. Muttiah Muralitharan and Glenn McGrath each named him the most dangerous or the greatest batsman they ever bowled to.

Bowling was another matter. He turned his arm over in Tests from time to time, and the wicket column stayed politely blank. It is hard to imagine he lost any sleep over it.

Away from the middle

In Trinidad he grew up playing football with friends who went on to the 2006 World Cup, Dwight Yorke, Shaka Hislop and Russell Latapy among them, and he later turned out in Soccer Aid. He was named BBC Overseas Sports Personality of the Year, a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and an honorary member of Australia's national order, and he was made Trinidad and Tobago's Ambassador for Sport. A stadium in Trinidad, opened in 2017, carries his name.

After his playing days he coached batting for Sunrisers Hyderabad in the IPL.

And finally

After his last international match, at the 2007 World Cup, he asked the crowd whether he had entertained them. The roar that came back answered for everyone who ever watched him bat.
